As for the Meccan part: it is from the thirtieth verse of it to its end.

As for the Medinan part: it is from the twenty-fifth verse to the thirtieth.

As for the nocturnal (laylī) part: it is from its beginning to the end of five verses.

As for the diurnal (nahārī) part: it is from the fifth verse [in some copies: "from the fifth verse"] to the ninth verse.

As for the traveling (safarī) part: it is from the ninth verse to the twelfth.

As for the settled (ḥaḍarī) part: it is up to the twentieth verse [of it], and it was attributed to Medina because of the nearness of its period.

His saying, ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾: that is, beware of His punishment. ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾. The zalzalah (convulsion) is movement in a terrifying state.

Concerning the time of this convulsion there are two views:

The first: that it is on the Day of Resurrection, after the raising up. ʿImran ibn Husayn reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, "﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾," and said: "Do you know what day that is? It is the day when the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, will say to Adam, peace be upon him: 'Send forth the group for the Fire.'" Then he mentioned the hadith. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [p. 403] "Allah the Exalted will say to Adam on the Day of Resurrection: 'Arise, and send forth the group of the Fire.' He will say: 'O Lord, what is the group of the Fire?' He will say: 'Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire. Then the infant will turn gray, and every pregnant woman will drop her burden.'" And he recited the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: The convulsion of the Hour is its establishment, meaning that it is close to the establishment of the Hour and will be with it. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: This convulsion will occur on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: that it will occur in this world before the Resurrection, and it is among the portents of the Hour. This was said by 'Alqamah, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn Jurayj. Abu al-'Aliyah reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Six signs before the Resurrection: while people are in their markets, the light of the sun will go away. While they are in that state, the stars will scatter. While they are in that state, the mountains will fall upon the face of the earth, and they will shake and quake. The jinn will flee to mankind, and mankind to the jinn, and the beasts, birds and wild animals will mingle, and some of them will surge over others. The jinn will say to mankind: 'We will bring you the news,' so they will set off to the seas, and behold, they are fire blazing. While they are in that state, the earth will split open down to the seventh earth, and the heaven down to the seventh heaven. While they are in that state, the wind will come to them and they will die." Muqatil said: This convulsion is before the first blast of the Trumpet, because a caller will call out from the heaven: "O people, the command of Allah has come!" They will be struck with a severe terror, so the young will turn gray and the pregnant will drop their burdens.

His saying, ﴿a tremendous thing﴾: that is, it cannot be described because of its greatness.

His saying, ﴿The Day you see it﴾, meaning the convulsion, ﴿every nursing mother will neglect what she nursed﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: she will forget her child and abandon it. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: she will be preoccupied with it. This was said by Qutrub, and from it is the saying of Ibn Rawaha:

"And it makes the friend forget his friend."

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read تُذْهِلُ (tudhilu) with a raised tā' and a kasra on the hā', and كُلَّ (kulla) with a fatha on the lām. Al-Akhfash said: He said مُرْضِعَةٍ (mursi'a, "nursing mother") because he intended the action, and if he had intended the attribute, as far as we can see, he would have said مُرْضِعٍ (mursi'). Al-Hasan said: The nursing mother will forget her child before weaning, and the pregnant woman will drop what is in her womb before its completion. This indicates that the convulsion occurs in this world, because after the raising up there is no pregnancy.

His saying, ﴿And you see the people as intoxicated﴾. 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ya'mur read وَتُرَى (wa-tura, "and they are seen") with a damma on the tā'. The meaning of سُكارى (sukara, "intoxicated") here is: from the intensity of fear. ﴿But they are not intoxicated﴾ by wine. The meaning is: you see the people as if they were drunk from the bewilderment of their minds, because of the severity of what passes over them; they stagger like one drunk on wine. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read سَكْرى (sakra) and وَما هم بِسَكْرى (wa-ma hum bi-sakra), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Farra' said: It is a good reading, because it is like "the slain" (halka) and "the wounded" (juraha). 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read سُكارى وما هم بِسُكارى (sukara wa-ma hum bi-sukara) with a fatha on the sīn and the rā' and with the alif affirmed. ﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe﴾. In this there is evidence that their intoxication is from fear of His punishment.

His saying, ﴿And among the people is he who disputes about Allah﴾. The exegetes said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Concerning what he disputed there are three views:

The first: that whenever some part of the Qur'an was revealed he denied it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he claimed the angels were the daughters of Allah. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: that he said Allah is not able to bring the dead back to life. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾: that is, he says it only through the misleading of Satan, not through knowledge. ﴿And follows﴾ whatever he beautifies for him, ﴿every rebellious devil﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of "rebellious" (marid) in Surah al-Nisa' [4:117].

His saying, ﴿It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally﴾: كُتِبَ (kutiba, "it has been decreed") means قُضِيَ (quḍiya, "it has been determined"). The pronoun in عَلَيْهِ ("upon him") and in تَوَلاهُ ("takes him as an ally") refers to Satan. The meaning of the verse is: it has been determined for Satan that he will lead astray whoever follows him. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read كَتَبَ (kataba) with a fatha on the kāf, and أَنَّهُ (anna-hu) with a fatha on the hamza, [and فَإنَّهُ (fa-inna-hu) with a kasra on the hamza]. Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ya'mur read إِنَّهُ (inna-hu) and فَإِنَّهُ (fa-inna-hu) with a kasra on the hamza in both. We have already explained the meaning of "the Blaze" (al-sa'ir) in Surah al-Nisa' [4:10].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 5–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind﴾, meaning: the people of Makkah, ﴿if you are in doubt about the resurrection﴾; that is, in doubt about the Resurrection, ﴿then indeed We created you from dust﴾, meaning: the creation of Adam, ﴿then from a drop (nutfah) of semen﴾, meaning: the creation of his offspring. The meaning is: if you doubt your being resurrected, then reflect on the matter of your creation and your origin, for you will find no difference in power between the beginning and the return. As for the nutfah, it is the semen (al-mani). The 'alaqah is thick, congealed blood. It has been said that it was called 'alaqah because of its moistness and its clinging to whatever it passes through; when it dries, it is no longer 'alaqah. The mudghah is a small piece of flesh. Ibn Qutaybah said: it was so named because it is about the amount that is chewed (yumdagh), just as it is said ghurfah for the amount that is scooped (yughraf).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿formed and unformed﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

The first: the formed (mukhallaqah) is that which was created well-proportioned, and the unformed (ghayr mukhallaqah) is what the wombs expel of the drops, which is blood before it becomes a created form. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: the formed is that whose creation was completed by the breathing of the spirit into it, which is the one born alive at full term, and the unformed is what falls out not alive, its creation not completed by the breathing of the spirit into it. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the formed is the shaped (musawwarah), and the unformed is the unshaped, not formed. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: the formed and the unformed are both the miscarriage (siqt): sometimes it falls as a drop and a clot, sometimes part of it has been shaped, and sometimes all of it has been shaped. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: the formed is the complete (tammah), and the unformed is the miscarriage. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

The first: We created you so that We may make clear to you what you do and what you leave undone.

The second: so that We may make clear to you in the Qur'an the beginning of your creation and the changing of your states.

The third: so that We may make clear to you the perfection of Our wisdom and Our power in turning over the states of your creation.

The fourth: so that We may make clear to you that the resurrection is true.

Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited (liyubayyina lakum) with a yaʼ.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We cause to remain in the wombs﴾. Abu Raja' and Ibn Mas'ud recited (wa-yuqarru) with a raised yaʼ, a fathah on the qaf and a dammah on the ra'. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i recited (wa-yuqirru) with a raised yaʼ, a kasrah on the qaf and a fathah on the ra'. What remains in the wombs is that which is not a miscarriage. ﴿until an appointed term﴾, which is the term of birth. ﴿Then We bring you out as a child﴾.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is in the place of (aṭfāl), plural children, and the Arabs sometimes place the singular form in the sense of the plural. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿and the angels after that are supporters﴾ (al-Tahrim: 4); that is, supporters (ẓuhara'). And he recited:

"We said: 'Submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of enmities.'"

And he also recited:

"In your throats there is a bone, and we have been choked."

Others said: He said ﴿a child﴾ in the singular, because the mim in His saying ﴿We bring you out﴾ already indicates the plural, so there was no need to say children (aṭfālan).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then that you may reach﴾. There is an implied element here; its estimate is: then We let you live long so that you may reach your full maturity (ashuddakum). The meaning of al-ashudd (full maturity) has already been mentioned (al-An'am: 153). ﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾ before reaching full maturity, ﴿and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, which we have explained in (al-Nahl: 70). Then God, exalted is He, showed them His reviving of the dead by His reviving of the earth, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, dead and dry. Similar is "the fire became lifeless" (hamadat al-nar), when it is extinguished and goes out.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so when We send down upon it water﴾, meaning: rain, ﴿it stirs﴾; that is, it moves for vegetation, because it swells up when plants appear, and this is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it grows﴾; that is, it rises and increases. Al-Mubarrad said: he meant: its vegetation stirred and grew, so he omitted the annexed noun. Al-Farra' said: Abu Ja'far al-Madani recited (wa-ra'at) with a hamzah with a fathah after the ba'. If he intended the ruba'iyyah, the one who guards the people (i.e., the lookout, who rises high to watch), that is, it rises up; otherwise it is an error.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it causes to grow from every beautiful pair﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: from every good kind that delights (yubhij), that is, gladdens (yusurr), and it is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: the matter is that, as it has been described to you. The better reading is that the position of ﴿that﴾ is nominative (raf'), but it may also be accusative in the sense of: God did that because it is the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the Hour﴾; that is, and so that you may know that the Hour is coming.

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 22, verses 8–10:

God's words: ﴿And among people is one who argues﴾. Its explanation has already passed. This too was revealed concerning al-Nadr. Al-huda (guidance) means clear evidence and proof.

God's words: ﴿turning aside his side﴾. Al-ʿitf is the side. The two ʿitfs of a man are his two sides, the right and the left. It is the place that a person bends and twists when he turns away from walking. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿thāniya﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and its meaning is with tanwin, meaning: "turning his side." It is reported in the exegesis that its meaning is "twisting his neck," and this is a description of the arrogant. The meaning is: "Among people is one who argues without knowledge, arrogantly."

God's words: ﴿so that he may lead astray﴾. That is, so that his affair ends in misguidance. Even though he may not be able to lead anyone astray, his affair will end in that. ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾, which is what befell him on the day of Badr, for he was killed. What follows this has already been explained [Yunus: 70] up to God's words: ﴿And among people is one who worships God on an edge﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿upon an edge﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: "upon doubt." Abu Ubaydah said: "Everyone who is in doubt about something is upon an edge, not firm and not lasting." This is clarified by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If good befalls him﴾, that is, ease and well-being, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾ in the worship of Allah. ﴿But if an ordeal befalls him﴾, a test by drought and scarcity of wealth, ﴿he turns back on his face﴾; that is, he returns from his religion to disbelief. The meaning is: he turns back to the direction from which he came, which is disbelief. ﴿He loses the world﴾, since he does not attain what he sought from it, ﴿and the Hereafter﴾ he loses by apostasy from the religion.

Abu Razin al-Uqayli, Abu Mijlaz, Mujahid, Talhah ibn Musarrif, Ibn Abi Ablah, and Zayd on the authority of Ya'qub read: (khasira al-dunya) with an alif before the sin and with a fatha on the ra' (khasira is the form of the verb, as written in the reading), and (wal-ākhirata) with a kasra on the ta'. ﴿He calls upon﴾ this apostate, that is, he worships, ﴿that which does not harm him﴾ if he does not worship it, ﴿nor benefit him﴾ if he obeys it. ﴿That is﴾ what he did, ﴿is the far-off error﴾ from the truth. ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. Al-Zajjaj related from the people of Basra and Kufa that the lam carries the sense of postponement, and the meaning is: he calls upon one for whose harm (is nearer than his benefit). He said: The explanation of this is that the lam is the lam of oath and emphasis, and its proper place is at the beginning of the speech, so it was moved forward to be placed in its right position. Al-Suddi said: his harm in the Hereafter through his worship of it is nearer than his benefit.

If it is said: Is there any benefit in worshipping an idol?

The answer: There is no benefit from it at all, but it came in the language of the Arabs, who say of a thing that does not exist: "this is far-off."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Surely an evil patron, and surely an evil companion!﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: al-mawla is the protector (al-waliyy), and al-ashir is the companion and intimate friend (al-khalil).

So He addressed this verse to both groups. Then concerning the meaning of this victory there are two opinions:

The first: it is domination (al-ghalaba), said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and by the majority.

The second: it is provision (al-rizq), related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾. Concerning what is meant by "the sky" there are two opinions:

The first: the ceiling of his house. The meaning is: let him tie a rope to the ceiling of his house, and let him hang himself with it, ﴿then let him cut off﴾ the rope so that he dies strangled. This is the view of the majority. The meaning of the verse is: let him imagine this matter in himself, not that he actually does it, because if he is strangled he cannot see or know.

The second: it is the well-known sky, and the meaning is: let him cut off revelation from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ if he is able. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then let him cut off﴾ (thumma li-yaqta')—Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read it with a kasra on the lam: (thumma li-yaqta'), (thumma li-yaqḍū) [al-Hajj: 29]. Ibn Amir added: (wa-li-yūfū) [al-Hajj: 29], (wa-li-yaṭṭawwafū) [al-Hajj: 29], also with a kasra on the lam. Ibn Kathir put a kasra on the lam only in (thumma liyaqḍū). Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read these lams with sukun, and likewise throughout the Qur'an whenever they are preceded by a waw, fa', or thumma. al-Farra' said: Whoever uses sukun has lightened it, and most of the speech of the Arabs is to use sukun with every imperative lam joined by a waw or fa', though some have used a kasra. Abu Ali said: The original is the kasra, because when you begin you say: li-yaqum Zayd (let Zayd stand).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Will his scheming remove his rage?﴾ Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is: will his cunning remove his rage? The meaning is: let him exert his utmost effort.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus﴾, i.e., and like that which has preceded of the verses of the Qur'an, (p-415) "We have sent it down," meaning the Qur'an. What follows is clear up to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾, i.e., He will decide among them ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ by admitting the believers to Paradise and the others to the Fire. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things﴾ of their deeds ﴿Witness﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the moving creatures?﴾ That is: Do you not know? We have already explained in Surat an-Nahl (16:49) the meaning of prostration with regard to those who have intellect and those who do not.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And many among the people﴾ means: the monotheists who prostrate to Allah.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And many have deserved the punishment﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: they are the disbelievers, and they do prostrate, but their prostration is the prostration of their shadows. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: they do not prostrate, and the meaning is: "And many among the people refused prostration, so the punishment became due upon them for their abandoning prostration." This is the saying of al-Farra' (ʿAbd Allah ibn Ziyad al-Farra', the grammarian).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, there is no one to honor him﴾; that is: whoever Allah causes to be wretched, there is no one to make him happy. ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ with His creation, of honor and humiliation. (p-416)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 19–22:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are two adversaries (khasmān) who dispute concerning their Lord﴾. Scholars differed regarding who this verse was revealed about, in four opinions:

The first: It was revealed concerning the group who fought in single combat at the Battle of Badr: Hamza, ʿAli, ʿUbayd ibn al-Harith, ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabiʿa, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtba. This is the view of Abu Dharr.

The second: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book. They said to the believers: "We are more entitled to God and older than you in scripture, and our prophet came before your prophet." The believers said: "We are more entitled to God. We believed in Muhammad, and we believed in your prophet and in what God sent down of scripture, while you know our prophet, yet you disbelieved in him out of envy." Then this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada.

The third: It refers to all the believers and the disbelievers. This meaning was held by al-Hasan, ʿAta' and Mujahid. (p-417)

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the dispute between Paradise and Hell. Hell said: "God created me for His punishment," and Paradise said: "God created me for His mercy." This was said by ʿIkrima.

As for His saying, ﴿These (hādhān)﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, ʿIkrima and Ibn Kathir recited it as "hāddhān" with the nun shaddah, followed by ﴿two adversaries (khasmān)﴾. Its meaning is: two groups (jamʿān), and they are not two men. For this reason He said, ﴿they dispute (ikhtaṣamū)﴾, and did not say "ikhtaṣamā." It is also reported that Ibn Masʿud and Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "ikhtaṣamā."

Concerning their dispute there are three opinions:

The first: It is over the religion of their Lord, and this is according to the first two opinions. The second: It is over the Resurrection, said by Mujahid. The third: that it is a dispute of boasting, according to the view of ʿIkrima.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾; that is, they will be prepared and made into clothing. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Shirts of fire." Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "What is meant by fire here is copper (nuḥās)." As for ﴿the boiling water (ḥamīm)﴾, it is hot water, ﴿by which will be melted (yuṣhar bihi)﴾. Al-Farra' said: "It is melted by it; one says, 'I melted the fat with fire (ṣahartu al-shaḥm bi-l-nār)'." The exegetes said: By the hot water will be melted what is in their bellies of fat or intestines, until it comes out from their posteriors, and the skins will be roasted and fall off from its heat. ﴿And for them are maqāmiʿ (rods of iron)﴾. Al-Dahhak said: these are hammers. Al-Hasan said: The fire will hurl them with its flames, and when they are at its top they will be struck with maqāmiʿ, and they will fall into it for seventy autumns; then when they reach its bottom, the roar of its blaze will strike them, and they will not rest for an hour. Muqatil said: When Hell seethes it will cast them up to its top, and they will wish to come out, but the guardians of Hell will meet them with maqāmiʿ and strike them, so that one of them falls from that blow down to its depths. Others said: When the fire pushes them, they think it will cast them out of it, but the Zabaniyya return them with rods of iron.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And pearls﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wa-lu'lu'in) in the genitive (bi-l-khafd). Nafi' and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read (wa-lu'lu'an) in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: according to the one who reads it in the genitive, the meaning is: they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and of pearls; according to the one who reads it in the accusative, the meaning is: and they will be adorned with pearls.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they were guided﴾; that is, they were guided in the world ﴿to the good of speech﴾. On this there are three opinions:

The first: that it is "There is no god but Allah, and praise be to Allah." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Zayd added: "and Allah is the Greatest."

The second: the Qur'an. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. This is related by al-Mawardi.

As for ﴿the path of the Praiseworthy﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the way of Islam.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verse 25:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and [they] bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾; that is, they prevent people from entering Islam. Al-Zajjaj said: The word "yasuddun" (they bar) is in the present tense, and it is coordinated with the past-tense form, because the meaning of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is "those who are disbelievers." So it is as if He said: "Indeed the disbelievers and those who bar [others]…" As for the predicate of "inna" (indeed), it is omitted, so the meaning is: "Indeed those whose attribute is this have perished."

Regarding "al-Masjid al-Haram" (the Sacred Mosque) there are two opinions:

One: the entire Sanctuary (al-Haram). Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "They used to regard the whole Haram as a mosque."

The second: the mosque itself, related by al-Mawardi.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿which We have made for the people﴾. Here is the complete pause (waqf al-tamam).

On its meaning there are two opinions:

One: We made it for all people; We did not restrict it to some of them rather than others. This is according to the view that it refers to the entire Haram.

The second: We made it a qibla (direction of prayer) for their prayers and a place of rites (mansak) for their pilgrimage. This is according to the view that it refers to the mosque itself. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ibn Abi Ablah, and Hafs from Asim read ﴿sawa'an﴾ (equal) in the accusative, so the pause falls on "sawa'an," and some reciters did pause in this way. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "al-'Akif" (the resident) and "al-Badi" (the visitor) are in apposition (badal) to "al-nas" (the people), inasmuch as they are comprehensive of them, so the meaning becomes: "which We have made equal for the resident and the visitor." As for "al-'Akif," it is the one who stays; and "al-Badi" is the one who comes to it from outside its people. This is from their saying "badā al-qawm" (the people went out), when they left the settled areas for the open desert.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "al-Badi" with a yā' (ي), except that Ibn Kathir paused with a yā', while Abu Amr paused without a yā'. Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and al-Musayyibi from Nafi' read it without a yā' in both states.

Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two opinions:

One: the resident and the visitor are equal in dwelling in Makka and settling in it, so neither of them has more right to a dwelling than the other, except that no one may be evicted from his house. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada. Abu Hanifa and Ahmad took a similar position, and the school of these scholars holds that renting and selling the houses of Makka is forbidden. This is according to the view that "the mosque" means the entire Haram.

The second: they are equal in its virtue, its sanctity, and the performance of the rites within it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid. Some scholars permitted the sale of houses in Makka, and al-Shafi'i held this view. According to this, "the mosque" may mean the Haram, and it may also mean the mosque itself.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and whoever intends therein with deviation﴾. In language, "ilhad" (deviation) means turning away from the right course. The "ba'" (ب) here is superfluous (za'ida), as in His words: ﴿grows with the oil﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 20). They also recited:

Into a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows the shatt (a bitter shrub), and whose lower part grows the markh and the shabahan (types of plants).

The meaning is: "and its lower part grows the markh." Another said:

They are free women, not the owners of wine-jars, with black eyelids, who do not recite the surahs.

Another said:

We are the sons of Ja'da, lords of the irrigated land; we strike with the sword and hope for relief.

This is the view of the majority of the linguists. Ibn Qutayba said: The "ba'" may be added in speech, as in this verse, and as in His words: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ (al-'Alaq: 1); ﴿and shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ (Maryam: 25); ﴿which of you is the afflicted one﴾ (al-Qalam: 6); ﴿you send them tidings with affection﴾ (al-Mumtahana: 1); ﴿a spring from which the servants drink﴾ (al-Insan: 6), meaning "drink it." "Min" may also be added, as in His words: ﴿I do not desire any provision from them﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 57). "Al-lam" may be added, as in His words: ﴿those who fear their Lord﴾ (al-A'raf: 154). The "kaf" (ك) may be added, as in His words: ﴿there is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shura: 11). "'An" may be added, as in His words: ﴿those who oppose His command﴾ (al-Nur: 63). "Inna" may be added, as in His words: ﴿indeed it will meet you﴾ (al-Jumu'a: 8). The light "in" (إن) may be added, as in His words: ﴿in that which We had established you in﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 26). "Ma" may be added, as in His words: ﴿after a little while they will surely become regretful﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 40). And the "waw" may be added, as in His words: ﴿and He had thrown him down upon his forehead﴾ and ﴿and We called to him﴾ (al-Saffat: 103-104).

Regarding what is meant by this deviation, there are five opinions:

First: it is wrongdoing (zulm). This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: it is committing an evil deed. According to this, all sins are included. It has been narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Do not hoard food in Makka, for hoarding food in Makka is deviation through wrongdoing."

Second: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan and Qatada said likewise.

Third: it is shirk and killing. This was said by Ata'.

Fourth: it is making lawful the prohibitions of the state of ihram (sacred state of pilgrimage). This meaning is also reported from Ata'.

Fifth: it is deliberately making the forbidden lawful. This was said by Ibn Juraij.

If it is asked: Is a person held accountable if he intends wrongdoing in Makka but does not commit it?

The answer has two aspects:

One: if he resolves upon that within the Haram specifically, he is punished. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 34–35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and some of the companions of Abu 'Amr read the vowel of the sin as a kasra (manasik-style, mansik). The rest read it with a fatha. Whoever reads it with a fatha intends the verbal noun (masdar) from nasaka, yansuku (to perform worship). Whoever reads it with a kasra intends the place of the rite, like majlis (place of sitting) and matla' (place of rising). The meaning of the verse: for every believing community among the earlier nations We appointed the slaughter of sacrifices, ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the beasts of livestock﴾. He specified the beasts of livestock because they are the ones prescribed for drawing near to Allah. The purpose of the verse is that sacrificial slaughter was not exclusive to this community, and that mentioning the name of Allah over it was prescribed before this community.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So your God is one God﴾; that is, it is not fitting that you mention other than Him over your sacrifices. ﴿So to Him submit﴾; that is, comply and humble yourselves. We have already mentioned the meaning of ikhbat (humble submission) in (Hud: 23), and likewise the wording of the verse that follows this one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 36–37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the camels (al-budn)﴾. al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read it with a raised *dal*. al-Farra' said: It is said *budn* and *budum*, and the lightened form is better and more common, because every plural whose singular is on the pattern *fa'alah*, when the first letter of its plural is vowelled with *damma*, is lightened, like *akamah* and *ukm*, *ajamah* and *ujm*, and *khashabah* and *khushb*. al-Zajjaj said: *al-budn* is in the accusative by a hidden verb that is explained by the one that appears, and the meaning is "and We made the camels (into symbols)." If you wish, you may raise it as a new sentence, but the accusative is better. It is said *budn*, *budum*, and *badanah*, like your saying *thumr*, *thumur*, and *thamarah*. It was called *badanah* because it becomes fat (*tabdun*), that is, it grows fat. (p-432)

The exegetes have two opinions regarding *al-budn*:

The first: they are camels and cows. This is what 'Ata' said.

The second: only camels. al-Zajjaj related this, and said: The first is the view of most of the jurists of the major cities. al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: *al-badanah* is a term which, in the language, is specific to camels, but the cow takes its place in ruling, because the Prophet (ﷺ) made a *badanah* equal to seven (shares) and a cow equal to seven (shares).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah﴾; that is, We have made for you in them an act of worship to Allah: from driving them to the House, garlanding them, marking them, slaughtering them, and feeding from them. ﴿For you in them is good﴾, which is benefit in this world and reward in the Hereafter. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them﴾; that is, over their slaughtering. ﴿Standing in lines (sawaff)﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah read *sawafin* with a *nun*. al-Hasan, Abu Majlaz, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ya'mur read *sawafi* with a *ya'*. al-Zajjaj said: *sawaff* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), but it is not given nunation because it is not declined; that is, its legs have been arranged in a row. The meaning: mention the name of Allah over them while they are being slaughtered. A camel is slaughtered while standing, and this verse indicates that. As for whoever reads *sawafin*, the *saffin* is the one that stands on three legs; when they wish to slaughter a camel, one of its forelegs is tied, and so it is *saffin*, and the plural is *sawafin*. Furthermore, whoever reads *sawafi* with a *ya'* and with a *fathah* without nunation, its explanation is "pure" (*khawalis*), that is, sincerely for Allah, so do not associate anyone with Him in the mention of His name over their slaughtering. ﴿So when their sides fall (wajabat junubuha)﴾; that is, when they fall to the ground. It is said: *wajaba al-ha'it wajbah*, meaning the wall collapsed when it fell, and *wajaba al-qalb wajiban*, meaning the heart beat violently from fear. Know that slaughtering them standing is a sunnah, and what is meant by their falling on their sides is their death. The command to eat from them is a command of permission, and this is about the sacrificial animals. (p-433)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And feed the contented (al-qani') and the beggar (al-mu'tarr)﴾. al-Hasan read *al-mu'tarri* with a *kasrah* on the *ra'* and lightened. Regarding these two words there are six opinions:

The first: *al-qani'* is the one who asks, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who presents himself but does not ask. This was narrated by Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise, and al-Farra' preferred it.

The second: *al-qani'* is the one who refrains (*al-mut'affif*), and *al-mu'tazz* is the one who asks. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah and al-Nakha'i said likewise, and from al-Hasan there are two similar opinions.

The third: *al-qani'* is the one who is content with what you have given him while he is in his house, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches you and visits you without asking. al-'Awfi narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: *al-qani'* is your neighbour who is content with what you have given him, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who presents himself without asking. This is the view of al-Qurazi. According to this, the meaning of *al-qani'* is that he is content with what is given to him. Whoever says it is the one who refrains says it is the one who is content with what he has.

The fourth: *al-qani'* is the people of Makkah, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who comes to them from outside the people of Makkah. Khasif narrated this from Mujahid.

The fifth: *al-qani'* is the neighbour, even if he is wealthy, and *al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches you. Layth narrated this from Mujahid.

The sixth: *al-qani'* is the needy one who asks, and *al-mu'tarr* is the friend who visits. Zayd ibn Aslam said this. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said *qana'a yaqna'u qunuban* when he asked, and *qani'a yaqna'u qana'ah* when he was content. It is said of *al-mu'tarr*: *i'taranee*, *i'taranee*, and *'arranee*. al-Zajjaj said: The view of the people of language is that *al-qani'* is the one who asks; it is said *qana'a yaqna'u qunuban* when he asked, so he is *qani'*. Ash-Shammakh said:

*"The wealth of a man, when it sets him right, makes him rich in his needs, more chaste than begging."*

That is, more than asking. It is also said *qani'a qana'ah* when he was content, so he is *qani'*, and *al-mu'tarr* and *al-mu'tari* are the same. (p-434)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus﴾; that is, like what We described of their slaughtering standing, ﴿We have subjected them to you﴾, as a blessing from Us upon you, so that you may be able to slaughter them in the prescribed manner, ﴿that perhaps you may give thanks﴾; that is, so that you may give thanks.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their flesh will not reach Allah﴾. 'Asim al-Jahdari, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ya'qub read *lan tanala Allaha luhumuha* with a *ta'*, and *lakin tanaluhu al-taqwa* also with a *ta'*.

This is a warning that deeds are not accepted when they are devoid of sound intention.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus He has subjected them﴾, whose explanation has already passed (al-Hajj: 37). ﴿That you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾; that is, for what He has made clear to you and directed you to the landmarks of His religion and the rites of His pilgrimage. This is that one says: "Allah is the Greatest" for having guided us. ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: That means the monotheists.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How many a town We destroyed﴾. Abu 'Amr recited "ahlaktuhā" (I destroyed it) with the tā' (first person singular), while the rest recited "ahlaknāhā" (We destroyed it) with the nūn (first person plural).

The second: it is tall. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil. In the speech there is an ellipsis; its estimated form is: "and a palace high-built, abandoned as well, in which there is no inhabitant."

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 22, verses 52–55:

Allah's words: ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger﴾, to the end of the verse. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: The occasion of its revelation was that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had the Surah al-Najm (The Star) revealed to him, he recited it until he reached His words: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza? And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm 53:19–20]. Then Satan cast upon his tongue: "Those are the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq al-ula), and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for." When the Quraysh heard this, they rejoiced. Then Jibril came to him and said: "What have you done? You recited to the people what I did not bring you from Allah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ grieved a great deal, so this verse was revealed to comfort his heart and to inform him that a similar thing had happened to the prophets before him.

The verifying scholars (al-ulama al-muhaqqiqun) said: This does not hold true, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is protected (ma'sum) from such a thing. Even if it were sound, the meaning would be that some of the devils of mankind uttered those words, for when he recited they would make noise and din, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it"﴾ [Fussilat 41:26].

He said: Regarding the meaning of ﴿tamanna﴾ (wished/recited) there are two views:

The first: it means "recited." This is what most of them said, and they cited (poetry):

"He wished for the Book of Allah at the beginning of his night and its end, and met the death-appointed fate of destiny."

And another said:

"He wished for the Book of Allah at the end of his night, the wishing of Dawud for the Zabur at a steady pace."

(p-٤٤٣)

The second: that it is from the "umniyyah" (wish, desire). This is that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once wished that nothing from Allah would come to him that would cause his people to flee from him. Then Satan cast upon his tongue what he had wished for." This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

His words: ﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts﴾; that is, He nullifies it and removes it. ﴿Then Allah establishes His verses﴾. Muqatil said: He makes them firm (yuhkimuha) from falsehood.

His words: ﴿That He may make﴾. The lam is connected to His words: ﴿Satan casts﴾. Here "fitnah" (trial) means affliction and tribulation. "Maradh" (sickness) means doubt and hypocrisy. ﴿And the hardened of heart﴾ means those whose hearts are distant from faith.

Then He informed him that they are wrongdoers and that they are in constant opposition (shiqaq), and shiqaq means utmost enmity.

His words: ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know﴾, which is the tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and the Qur'an, and they are the believers. Al-Suddi said: It is the affirmation of Allah's abrogation (naskh, the repeal of one ruling or revelation by another).

His words: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to the abrogation of what Satan casts. The meaning is: that they may know that the abrogation of that and its nullification is truth from Allah, ﴿and so believe﴾ in the abrogation, ﴿and their hearts humble themselves to Him﴾; that is, submit and become humble. Then He explained through the rest of the verse that this faith and humility come only by the kindness and guidance of Allah. (p-٤٤٤)

His words: ﴿in doubt concerning it﴾; that is, in uncertainty.

Regarding the pronoun in "minhu" (concerning it), there are four views:

The first: it refers to His words: "those are the exalted cranes." The second: it refers to the prostration in Surah al-Najm. These two views are from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and the meaning would be: they say, "Why did he mention our gods and then retract his mention of them?" The third: it refers to the Qur'an, said by Ibn Jurayj. The fourth: it refers to the religion, related by al-Tha'labi.

His words: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them﴾, and regarding it there are two views:

The first: the Resurrection comes upon the polytheists who are disbelieving in it, said by al-Hasan.

The second: the hour of their death, mentioned by al-Wahidi.

His words: ﴿or there comes upon them the punishment of a barren day﴾. Regarding it there are two views:

The first: that it is the Day of Badr. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: that it is the Day of Resurrection, said by Ikrimah and al-Dahhak. The root of "al-uqm" is in childbirth. It is said: "a woman is 'aqim' (barren): she does not bear children," and "a man is 'aqim': no child is born to him." They cited:

"The women have become barren, so they bear none like him; indeed, women are barren in comparison to him."

(p-٤٤٥)

The wind is called "al-rih al-aqim" (the barren wind) by this name because it does not bring rain-bearing clouds. Thus this day is called "barren," because it brought no good.

According to the view of those who said it is the Day of Badr, there are three views regarding calling it "barren":

The first: that there was no blessing or good in it for the disbelievers, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: because they were not given respite into the night; rather, they were killed before evening, said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: because there is no equal to it in the greatness of its matter, due to the fighting of the angels in it, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

According to the view of those who said it is the Day of Resurrection, regarding its being so named there are two views:

The first: because it has no night, said by Ikrimah.

The second: because it brings nothing good or relief to the polytheists, mentioned by some of the exegetes.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verse 60–62:

Allah's words: ﴿That is so.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is, "The matter is that"; that is, the matter is what We have related to you.

﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾. The word 'uqubah (retaliation) means recompense, and the first act is not a retaliation in itself. It was called 'uqubah because the two actions are alike in the category of what is disliked, as in His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Since the requital was a harm inflicted on the one who received it, it was called an evil. A similar usage is: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. This was said by al-Hasan. The meaning of the verse is: whoever fights the polytheists as they fought him. ﴿Then he is wronged﴾; that is, he is wronged by being driven out of his home.

Muqatil claimed that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the polytheists of Makkah met the Muslims on a night that remained of the month of Muharram, and they fought them. The Muslims appealed to them not to fight in the sacred month, but they refused except to fight. The Muslims held firm, and Allah gave them victory over the polytheists. (p-447) The Muslims were troubled by fighting in the sacred month, so this verse was revealed, and He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning﴾ toward them ﴿and Forgiving﴾ for their fighting in the sacred month.

Allah's words: ﴿That﴾; that is, that victory, ﴿because Allah﴾, who is capable of whatever He wills. From His power is that He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and that Allah is Hearing of the supplication of the believers and Seeing of them, in that He placed faith and piety in them. ﴿That﴾, which He did of granting victory to the believers, is ﴿because Allah is the Truth﴾; that is, He is the true God. ﴿And that what they invoke﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read (yad'una) with the ya'. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with the ta'. The meaning is: and that what they worship ﴿besides Him is falsehood﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: the rain, ﴿and the earth becomes green﴾ with vegetation. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verse 67–70:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. It has already been explained earlier in this surah [al-Hajj: 34]. ﴿So let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾; that is, about the slaughtering of animals. This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh and Khuza'ah disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the matter of the slaughtered animal, saying: "How do you eat what you have killed yourselves, and not eat what Allah has killed?" They meant the carrion (maytah).

If it is said: since they were the ones disputing with him, how is it said: ﴿So let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾?

Al-Zajjaj has answered this, saying: The intended meaning is a prohibition addressed to him from disputing with them. So the meaning is: "Do not dispute with them." Just as you say to a man: "So-and-so should never dispute with you about this." This is permissible in a verb that can only occur between two parties, because argument and dispute are not complete except between two. So when you say: "So-and-so should not argue with you," it is equivalent to: "Do not argue with him." This does not apply in your saying: "So-and-so should not strike you," meaning: "Do not strike him." However, if you said: "So-and-so should not fight you (yudarribuka)," it would be like your saying: "Do not fight (with him)." This answer is supported by His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And invite to your Lord﴾; that is, to His religion and belief in Him. "Argued with you (jadalukaa)" means: disputed with you concerning the matter of the slaughtered animals. ﴿Then say: Allah knows best what you do﴾ of denial, so He will recompense you for it. ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾; that is, He will decide between you ﴿concerning that wherein you used to differ﴾ regarding religion; that is, you go in a direction opposite to what the believers follow. This is a good etiquette which Allah taught His servants, so that they may respond with it to one who argues out of obstinacy, and not answer him or debate with him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verse 67–70:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. It has already been explained earlier in this surah [al-Hajj: 34]. ﴿So let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾; that is, about the slaughtering of animals. This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh and Khuza'ah disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the matter of the slaughtered animal, saying: "How do you eat what you have killed yourselves, and not eat what Allah has killed?" They meant the carrion (maytah).

If it is said: since they were the ones disputing with him, how is it said: ﴿So let them not dispute with you about the matter﴾?

Al-Zajjaj has answered this, saying: The intended meaning is a prohibition addressed to him from disputing with them. So the meaning is: "Do not dispute with them." Just as you say to a man: "So-and-so should never dispute with you about this." This is permissible in a verb that can only occur between two parties, because argument and dispute are not complete except between two. So when you say: "So-and-so should not argue with you," it is equivalent to: "Do not argue with him." This does not apply in your saying: "So-and-so should not strike you," meaning: "Do not strike him." However, if you said: "So-and-so should not fight you (yudarribuka)," it would be like your saying: "Do not fight (with him)." This answer is supported by His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And invite to your Lord﴾; that is, to His religion and belief in Him. "Argued with you (jadalukaa)" means: disputed with you concerning the matter of the slaughtered animals. ﴿Then say: Allah knows best what you do﴾ of denial, so He will recompense you for it. ﴿Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾; that is, He will decide between you ﴿concerning that wherein you used to differ﴾ regarding religion; that is, you go in a direction opposite to what the believers follow. This is a good etiquette which Allah taught His servants, so that they may respond with it to one who argues out of obstinacy, and not answer him or debate with him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 73–74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O people, a parable has been struck﴾. Al-Akhfash said: If it is asked, "Where is the parable?"

The answer is that there is no parable here. The meaning is: "O people, a parable has been struck for me," that is, the idols have been likened to me. ﴿So listen﴾ to this parable. The interpretation of the verse is: the polytheists made the idols My partners, and they worshipped them along with Me. So listen to their condition. Then He clarified this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke﴾, that is, whom you worship, ﴿besides Allah﴾.

Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, and Ibn Abi Ablah read (yad'una) with an open yā'. Ibn al-Sumaifa', Abu Raja', and Asim al-Jahdari read (yud'awna) with a dammed yā' and an open 'ayn, meaning the idols. ﴿They will never create a fly﴾. The word dhubāb is singular. Its few-form plural is adhibbah, and its many-form plural is dhibbān, like ghurāb, aghribah, and ghirbān. It was said that He specified the fly because of its lowliness, its repulsiveness, and its abundance. ﴿Even if they gathered together for it﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿for it﴾, that is, for its creation. ﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them﴾, meaning from the idols. Ibn Abbas said: They used to smear their idols with saffron, which would dry, and the fly would come and snatch it. Ibn Jurayj said: When they perfumed their idols, they mixed their perfume with some sweets, such as honey and the like, and the fly would settle on it and snatch it from them, and neither the gods nor those who worshipped them could prevent that. Al-Suddi said: They used to set food before the gods, and the fly would settle on it and eat from it. Tha'lab said: He said ﴿they cannot rescue it from it﴾, thereby treating the actions of the gods as the actions of human beings, since they used to venerate them, slaughter for them, and address them, as in His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [an-Naml: 18]. When He addressed them, He made them like human beings. Similar is His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. We have explained this meaning under (al-A'raf: 191), at His saying: ﴿while they are created﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The seeker and the sought are weak﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: the seeker is the idol and the sought is the fly. This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the seeker is the fly, which seeks what it snatches of the perfume that is on the idol, and the sought is the idol, which seeks from the fly the stripping of what is on it. This was also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The third: the seeker is the worshipper of the idol, who seeks nearness through his worship, and the sought is the idol. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾, that is, they did not magnify Him with His true magnificence, when they made these idols partners to Him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong﴾, who is not overcome, ﴿Mighty﴾, who cannot be attacked.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 22, verses 77–78:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Bow down and prostrate yourselves﴾. The commentators (mufassirun) said: the meaning is "pray," because prayer is not performed except with bowing and prostration. ﴿And worship your Lord﴾; that is, make Him one (wahhidu-hu). **Section**

The scholars did not differ concerning the first prostration in (al-Hajj). They differed concerning this last prostration. It was narrated from Umar, Ibn Umar, Ammar, Abu al-Darda, Abu Musa, and Ibn Abbas that they said: "In (al-Hajj) there are two prostrations," and they said: "This surah was given preference over others by two prostrations." This is the view of our companions (the Hanbalis), and it is the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In (al-Hajj) there is one prostration." This is the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and Malik. What supports the first view is what Uqbah ibn Amir narrated: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, in (al-Hajj) are there two prostrations?' He said: 'Yes, and whoever does not prostrate for them, let him not recite them.'" (p-455)

**Section**

The scholars differed concerning the number of prostrations of the Qur'an. Two narrations are reported from Ahmad: one is that they are fourteen prostrations, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. The second is that they are fifteen, having added one prostration (Sad: 24). Abu Hanifa said they are fourteen: he removed the one at the end of (al-Hajj) and replaced it with the prostration of (Sad: 24).

**Section**

Prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa) is a sunnah. Abu Hanifa said it is obligatory (wajib). The prostration of recitation is not valid except with the opening takbir (takbirat al-ihram) and the salam, contrary to the companions of Abu Hanifa and some companions of al-Shafi'i. Bowing (ruku') does not suffice in place of the prostration of recitation, whereas Abu Hanifa said it suffices. The listener does not prostrate if the reciter does not prostrate; Ahmad stated this explicitly. It is disliked to recite the prostration verse in a prayer in which recitation is silent (salat al-ikhfat), contrary to al-Shafi'i.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And strive for Allah﴾. Regarding this striving there are three views:
One: it is the performance of all acts of obedience; this is the view of the majority. Two: it is fighting the disbelievers; this was said by al-Dahhak. Three: it is the struggle against the self and desire; this was said by Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak.

As for the due right of striving (haqq al-jihad), there are three views: (p-456)

One: it is exertion in the striving and exhausting of one's capacity in it. Two: it is sincerity of intention for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Three: it is doing what fulfills the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

**Section**

Some people claimed that this verse is abrogated (mansukh), and they differed concerning its abrogating verse, in two views:
One of them: His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (al-Baqarah: 286).
The second: His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (al-Taghabun: 16). Others said: rather, it is muhkam (not abrogated), and the first two views on the explanation of the due right of striving confirm this, and it is the more correct view, because Allah, Exalted, does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has chosen you﴾; that is, He selected you and chose you for His religion. Hardship (haraj) is constriction. Whatever difficulty a person falls into, there is in the Law a way out for it by repentance, expiation, or moving to a concession (rukhsah), and the like. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Hardship is what was upon the Children of Israel of burdens and severities, which Allah removed from this community."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham﴾. Al-Farra said: the meaning is: He has made it easy for you, like the religion of your father. When the kaf (like) is dropped, it is put in the accusative case (nusiba). The accusative may also be understood as an imperative, because the beginning of the speech is an command, which is His saying: ﴿Bow down and prostrate﴾, and "hold fast to the religion of your father."

If it is said: this address is to the Muslims, and Abraham is not the father of all of them?

The answer: if it is a general address to the Muslims, then he is like a father to them, because his sanctity and his right upon them is like the right of a child (over a father)... and if it is an address to the Arabs specifically, then Abraham is the father of all the Arabs; this is the view of the commentators. What appears to me is that the address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because Abraham is his father, and the community of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is included in what the Messenger of Allah was addressed with. (p-457)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He named you the Muslims﴾. Regarding the one referred to there are two views:
One: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority. On this view, regarding His saying ﴿before﴾ there are two views: one, before the revelation of the Qur'an He named you with this in the books He sent down. The second: "before" means in the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitab); and His saying ﴿and in this﴾ means in the Qur'an.

The second: it is Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿And from our offspring a Muslim community for You﴾ (al-Baqarah: 128). The meaning is: "before this time," which is in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, and "in this" is the time when he said: ﴿And from our offspring a Muslim community﴾. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾. The meaning: He chose you and named you so that the Messenger, meaning Muhammad ﷺ, may be ﴿a witness over you﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, that he has conveyed to you. We have explained this meaning in (al-Baqarah: 143), up to His saying: ﴿and give zakah﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: ask Him to protect you from everything that angers Him and that He dislikes. Al-Hasan said: hold fast to the religion of Allah. What follows this is explained in (al-Anfal: 40).

What supports the first view is what Uqbah ibn Amir narrated: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, in (al-Hajj) are there two prostrations?' He said: 'Yes, and whoever does not prostrate for them, let him not recite them.'" (p-455)

**Section**

The scholars differed concerning the number of prostrations of the Qur'an. Two narrations are reported from Ahmad: one is that they are fourteen prostrations, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i. The second is that they are fifteen, having added one prostration (Sad: 24). Abu Hanifa said they are fourteen: he removed the one at the end of (al-Hajj) and replaced it with the prostration of (Sad: 24).

**Section**

Prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa) is a sunnah. Abu Hanifa said it is obligatory (wajib). The prostration of recitation is not valid except with the opening takbir (takbirat al-ihram) and the salam, contrary to the companions of Abu Hanifa and some companions of al-Shafi'i. Bowing (ruku') does not suffice in place of the prostration of recitation, whereas Abu Hanifa said it suffices. The listener does not prostrate if the reciter does not prostrate; Ahmad stated this explicitly. It is disliked to recite the prostration verse in a prayer in which recitation is silent (salat al-ikhfat), contrary to al-Shafi'i.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And strive for Allah﴾. Regarding this striving there are three views:
One: it is the performance of all acts of obedience; this is the view of the majority. Two: it is fighting the disbelievers; this was said by al-Dahhak. Three: it is the struggle against the self and desire; this was said by Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak.

As for the due right of striving (haqq al-jihad), there are three views: (p-456)

One: it is exertion in the striving and exhausting of one's capacity in it. Two: it is sincerity of intention for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Three: it is doing what fulfills the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

**Section**

Some people claimed that this verse is abrogated (mansukh), and they differed concerning its abrogating verse, in two views:
One of them: His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (al-Baqarah: 286).
The second: His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ (al-Taghabun: 16). Others said: rather, it is muhkam (not abrogated), and the first two views on the explanation of the due right of striving confirm this, and it is the more correct view, because Allah, Exalted, does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has chosen you﴾; that is, He selected you and chose you for His religion. Hardship (haraj) is constriction. Whatever difficulty a person falls into, there is in the Law a way out for it by repentance, expiation, or moving to a concession (rukhsah), and the like. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Hardship is what was upon the Children of Israel of burdens and severities, which Allah removed from this community."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham﴾. Al-Farra said: the meaning is: He has made it easy for you, like the religion of your father. When the kaf (like) is dropped, it is put in the accusative case (nusiba). The accusative may also be understood as an imperative, because the beginning of the speech is an command, which is His saying: ﴿Bow down and prostrate﴾, and "hold fast to the religion of your father."

If it is said: this address is to the Muslims, and Abraham is not the father of all of them?

The answer: if it is a general address to the Muslims, then he is like a father to them, because his sanctity and his right upon them is like the right of a child (over a father)... and if it is an address to the Arabs specifically, then Abraham is the father of all the Arabs; this is the view of the commentators. What appears to me is that the address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because Abraham is his father, and the community of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is included in what the Messenger of Allah was addressed with. (p-457)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He named you the Muslims﴾. Regarding the one referred to there are two views:
One: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority. On this view, regarding His saying ﴿before﴾ there are two views: one, before the revelation of the Qur'an He named you with this in the books He sent down. The second: "before" means in the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitab); and His saying ﴿and in this﴾ means in the Qur'an.

The second: it is Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿And from our offspring a Muslim community for You﴾ (al-Baqarah: 128). The meaning is: "before this time," which is in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, and "in this" is the time when he said: ﴿And from our offspring a Muslim community﴾. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾. The meaning: He chose you and named you so that the Messenger, meaning Muhammad ﷺ, may be ﴿a witness over you﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, that he has conveyed to you. We have explained this meaning in (al-Baqarah: 143), up to His saying: ﴿and give zakah﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: ask Him to protect you from everything that angers Him and that He dislikes. Al-Hasan said: hold fast to the religion of Allah. What follows this is explained in (al-Anfal: 40).
